intro: People can talk without words. A red sign with eight sides says stop. A heart says love. A pin shows your club. These pictures are called symbols. In this unit, you will learn to read them.

Long ago, groups used symbols and codes too. Builders used a square and compass. A group in Italy put seven steps on a floor. Freemasons wrote notes in the pigpen code. You will try these ideas yourself.
You will make a class symbol. You will write your name in a secret code. You will also learn which secrets are happy and which ones you always tell a trusted grown-up.
bigQuestion: How do pictures, codes and secret words help a group share ideas?

timeline.t: Find a symbol on a sign or a building and say what it means.
Look at old symbols: the seven-step floor and the square and compass.
Talk with your class about what you all love.
Draw a simple class symbol together.
Make a key that matches each letter to a sign.
Write your name in the pigpen code.
Make up a class password and a quiet hand signal.
Sort happy secrets from unsafe ones, and name your trusted grown-ups.

words.d: a picture or shape that stands for an idea
a board with a picture, shape or words that gives a message
a small sign you wear to show a group you belong to
a tool with two legs, used to draw circles
a way to swap letters for shapes, numbers or other signs
a list that shows which sign goes with which letter
a secret word that lets you in or shows you belong
an adult who listens to you and helps keep you safe

test.q: A red heart on a card stands for what idea?
test.why: A heart is a symbol for love, like the heart on Sam's card.

choices: A picture that stands for an idea
test.why: A symbol is a picture that stands for an idea.

test.q: How many steps are shown on the old floor in Ostia, Italy?
test.why: The floor in Ostia shows seven pictures, one for each step.

test.q: Which tool is shaped like a letter L?
test.why: A builder's square is shaped like an L. It makes straight corners.

test.q: Why do club members wear the same pin?
test.why: Badges and pins show which group you belong to.

choices: It swaps letters for shapes or numbers
test.why: A code swaps letters for shapes, numbers or other signs.

test.q: In the pigpen code, what does the middle letter E look like?
test.why: E sits in the middle of the grid, so lines go all around it. It is a full box.

test.q: Why could Leo not read his sisters' note?
choices: He did not have the key
test.why: A key shows which sign goes with which letter. Leo had no key.

test.q: Which secret is a happy surprise?
choices: A secret that makes you scared
test.why: A birthday card is a surprise. It is a happy secret that will be shared soon.

test.q: A secret is about someone getting hurt. What do you do?
test.why: An unsafe secret is always told to a trusted grown-up. Telling is brave.

write.prompt: Think about codes and passwords. Are they a good thing for a club to have? Tell or write your answer. Use two things you learned, like the pigpen code, the builders' password or safe secrets.
tips: Tell one thing from the unit, like the pigpen key.
Tell a second thing, like the fort password.
Say what makes a secret happy or unsafe.
